title: We Get National Reading Test Results Every 2 Years. Writing? Try 20.
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler examines why the United States has no new national writing results since 2011 and will not until 2030. The 2017 NAEP writing results were never released because the switch from laptops to tablets created a mode difference, and the governing board now insists on a new writing framework before testing again. She finds that explanation unconvincing, since the framework has often gone unchanged for 15 years and classroom practice has moved closer to it. Her more distinctive move is to question whether a stand-alone writing test can measure writing at all, arguing that writing skill and content knowledge are inseparable and that prompts assuming no background knowledge quietly favour some children. She suggests using history-based prompts, but failing that urges the board to test again sooner with the existing framework and laptops, because silence on writing is worse than imperfect data.
points: Only 27 percent of eighth and twelfth graders were proficient in writing in 2011, yet writing is tested far less often than reading and math.
The 2017 results were withheld because tablets produced a mode effect, and the board's demand for a new framework pushes the next test to 2030.
Wexler argues writing and content knowledge are intertwined, so equalising background knowledge makes writing skill easier to measure than prompts that supposedly need none.
Separate reading and writing tests reinforce the harmful idea that these should be taught in isolation from each other and from history and science.
Imperfect NAEP writing data is still preferable to another decade of silence.
quotes: Reading and math are important, which is why Congress mandated those tests be given every two years as part of the National Assessment of Educational Progress, known as the NAEP. But writing is equally vital—and not just for success in college and the workplace. Writing can provide powerful boosts to reading comprehension, analytical thinking, and learning in general.

But as the results from NAEP writing tests in 2011 show, American students, on average, don’t write well. Only 27% of eighth- and twelfth-graders scored “Proficient” or above in writing in 2011, an even lower proficiency rate than the one for reading, where it’s hovered at around a third.

But apparently they did. A study found “a pattern of lower performance” on the 2017 writing tests that prevented the release of the results, which were deemed not comparable to those from 2011. A report looking into the 2017 results is still pending.

That, however, is only a problem if you believe you can evaluate those things separately. If, on the other hand, you see them as inextricably intertwined, you come to a different conclusion: The more you can equalize students’ background knowledge of a topic, the easier it is to isolate and measure differences in writing skill.

Giving separate writing tests—and reading tests—also reinforces the widespread and harmful idea that writing and reading comprehension should be taught in isolation from each other and from subjects like history and science. If those aspects of education were better integrated—and if teachers got better training in how to teach them—NAEP scores would almost certainly be much higher than they are, and gaps in scores would be narrower.

Tests like the NAEP can’t address or even identify what’s wrong with our education system. But they can at least sound a general alarm. That alarm rings loudly every two years for reading and math, leading to headlines and rounds of hand-wringing. The hoopla has its downsides, but it’s better than silence.
